prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are an invention in the sense the statutes and our own practice mean: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the trapping-light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once, and Jun Ye's group then carried the scheme to the 1e-18 regime. The original idea, the first strontium demonstration and the record accuracy are cleanly traceable to two named people, and the result has been verified over and over by independent laboratories in Japan, the US and Europe that now compare clocks at that level. It is also a tool that opens a door: gravitational redshift across millimetres, tests of the constancy of constants and a redefinition of the second are measurements that could not be made before. Four of eight members rank it in their top three, and three rank it first, so it is the only candidate with an unusually clear two-name attribution and no real credit dispute.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised by colleagues, is that clocks may look like a continuation of what the committee honoured in 2005 (the frequency comb) and in 2012 (single-ion control and clocks), so the discovery element could be seen as incremental. A second weakness is that I cannot verify from the supplied material how the credit should be divided between the original proposal, the first demonstration and the later accuracy record, and groups such as those of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Lemke are outside the credited set. The redefinition of the second has also not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still pending. Finally, topological insulators have far wider support in the opening round (five top-three placements, seven rankings), and I do not want to mistake my own first place for scientific merit relative to that breadth.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because progress is limited by measurement precision, but flags overlap with Ye's comb work (2005) and the ion-clock prize (2012), and prefers Kane, Mele and Molenkamp for topological insulators at rank five.
responses.response: I agree with the instrument argument and take the overlap worry seriously. My answer is that the discovery here is specific: the magic-wavelength condition lets a many-atom lattice reach ion-level systematic accuracy with far better statistics, which neither the comb nor the single-ion prize delivered. I do not want to hide that Ye's name appears in both lineages, so the citation should be anchored on the lattice clock itself and not on the comb. Where we differ is on topological insulators: I also put Kane, Mele and Molenkamp in my top two, so I do not see our views as far apart on that candidate.

responses.point: Lindroth values the unexpected, simple trick of the magic wavelength, stresses that a two-person configuration is clean, and notes that applications follow from the science. She also asks whether clocks are a continuation of the comb prize.
responses.response: I share the view that the two-person configuration is the strongest feature, and I note that no one has argued for a third name. I would qualify the claim that applications simply follow: the redefinition of the second is still pending, so I would avoid putting any practical-impact language in the citation and keep it to the measurement regime that was opened. On the continuation question I think the committee should decide it explicitly in round two instead of leaving it implicit, since it is the one issue that could lower support for this candidate.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks topological insulators first as a clean, general organising principle (a bulk invariant dictating boundary states) with experimental confirmation, arguing that recognition is overdue, and notes that the allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan is a real problem.
responses.response: I accept that the breadth and the overdue status make a strong case, and I do not claim lattice clocks outweigh it scientifically. My reservation is about attribution, not merit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect that Molenkamp's group then observed, and Zhang is not in the credited list, which leaves any three-person prize open to a later complaint. I would also want to know whether the committee sees the 2016 prize on topological phases as an obstacle. I agree with you that Molenkamp's HgTe observation is the original experiment; where we differ is that I would take Mele over Hasan, because the 3D ARPES work builds on, and is not the first sighting of, the topological edge state.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, as an experiment that surprised theory, and would credit theory, the decisive 2018 transport discovery and an early STM pioneer (Andrei).
responses.response: I find the experimental surprise and the speed of independent reproduction persuasive, and I ranked it third myself, partly because microscopy and spectroscopy were central to it. My hesitation is maturity: the pairing mechanism is still debated and the experiments are eight years old, so I would be more comfortable waiting. On attribution, I would not simply credit Andrei because she is a woman, and I think the record has to stand on its own: her STM work on van Hove singularities and flat bands is an early independent step, but Bistritzer's omission from a three-person prize is equally hard to justify, so the committee should weigh both before choosing the third name.

responses.point: Pearce, as Chair, ranks IceCube first as a detector-driven discovery with a clean single-name credit, and notes that Halzen is the originator but that the work was done by a very large collaboration.
responses.response: I agree that a detector-driven discovery is a good fit with how I think about the prize, and the diffuse flux is firmly established. My concern is attribution, which for me is the deciding test: a single-person prize for an instrument built and operated by a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA and DUMAND as precursors, requires us to be absolutely sure that Halzen alone did the original work, and I cannot be sure from what is in front of us. The source-class question is also still open. I would keep it as a strong candidate for the future but not as the configuration to build around this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
How to divide credit among the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium demonstration and the record-accuracy work, and whether any uncredited group has a claim of equal weight.
Whether a two-achievement configuration pairing clocks with topological insulators could be made fair, given that topological insulators would then be limited to one person.
Whether the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit makes any three-person topological insulator prize defensible.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I have no recorded co-authorship or institutional tie with Katori, Ye or the other credited names. I note only that committee colleague Goran Johansson is at Chalmers Physics and champions circuit QED, which I have not made my preferred part, and I have no stake in that candidate.
